newsitem.title: ISRAEL: FORECAST-Israel's April CPI seen rising 1.1 pct.
newsitem.headline: FORECAST-Israel's April CPI seen rising 1.1 pct.

text.p: Israel's April consumer price index (CPI), which will be released on Thursday, is expected to post a month-on-month rise of 1.1 percent, economists predicted on Wednesday.
This follows a 1.0 percent increase in March and a 1.7 percent jump in April 1996.
A climb of 1.1 percent in April would bring inflation in the past 12 months to 9.8 percent.

The Federation of Israeli Chambers of Commerce, which forecast a 1.1 percent rise in April, said housing prices are expected to post an increase of 1.1 percent. Higher prices for clothing, footwear, and fruit and vegetables also contributed to April inflation, the federation said.
It forecast inflation in all of 1997 would total 9.8 percent against 10.6 percent last year.
Bank Hapoalim, which also forecast a 1.1 percent spike in the April CPI, predicted inflation of 9.2 percent for 1997.

Jonathan Katz, senior economist at Sold Capital Markets, said that while his official forecast for April was 1.1 percent, "April's CPI could be surprisingly lower because there are some indications that housing prices may be corrected downwards and that may bring down the index".
In March, housing prices took a surprising jump, resulting in a higher-than-expected CPI.

"There's a faulty way of measuring housing prices in Israel and even the Central Bureau of Statistics (which calculates the CPI) is not satisfied with it and is planning to change the method," Katz said.
A 1.1 percent CPI rise in April, a seasonally high month for inflation, would be in line with the government's 1997 inflation target of 7-10 percent.
Katz said he did not believe a 1.1 percent hike would prompt the central bank to lower interest rates at the end of the month.
"But if it's 0.9 we could see some monetary easing," Katz said. "Recent trade figures support the continued (economic) slowdown theory, not the recovery that some people were talking about."
The Bank of Israel's key lending rate stands at 13.9 percent on an annual basis. Katz said a lowering of rates by the central bank -- if at all -- would not exceed 0.3 percentage point.
